extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether patent claims recite an abstract idea (Alice/Mayo framework) with categories and tests (fundamental economic practices; commercial/legal interactions; managing human activity; mental processes) and examiner-focused points A–D for mental-process determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Economic Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite fundamental economic practices (ways of organizing human economic activity) are directed to unpatentable abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case law: hedging to ‘protect against risk’ (Bilski v. Kappos, 561 U.S. 593) — hedging is a “fundamental economic practice” and an unpatentable abstract idea; methods allowing suppliers/consumers to minimize risk from market demand fluctuations; Bancorp Services v. Sun Life (claims for managing a stable value protected life insurance policy were an attempt to patent the abstract idea of managing such a policy and using well-known calculations); other examples include mitigating settlement risk (Alice v. CLS Bank), rules for conducting a wagering game (In re Smith), financial instruments designed to protect against investment risk (In re Chorna), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs. v. Amazon), local processing of payments for remotely purchased goods (Inventor Holdings v. Bed Bath Beyond), using an external marking on mail to communicate sender/recipient/contents (Secured Mail Solutions v. Universal Wilde), and placing an order based on displayed market information (Trading Technologies v. IBG). Courts treat these subject matters as abstract ideas under Alice/Mayo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or Legal Interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are about commercial interactions or legal interactions — agreements (contracts), legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities, or business relations — are often directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases and explanations: buySAFE (transaction performance guaranty: creating a contractual relationship was abstract); Bancorp (managing insurance via calculations); Accenture v. Guidewire (processing insurance claims under a policy); Fort Properties (aggregating real property and subjecting shares to a master agreement — tax-free exchanges were an abstract concept); Ultramercial (displaying ads in exchange for access — using advertising as exchange/currency viewed as an abstraction); Credit Acceptance (processing a credit application and creating financing packages viewed as ‘processing an application for financing a loan’ — abstract); Dealertrack (processing credit applications through a clearing-house relationship). The category includes agreements in contract form, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales behaviors, and business relationships; examiners should recognize these subject matters as potentially abstract under precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing Personal Behavior or Relationships or Interactions Between People
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting managing personal behavior, relationships, or interpersonal interactions (social activities, teaching, following rules/instructions) are categorized as abstract ideas related to organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and authority: tracking financial transactions to enforce pre-set spending limits (budgeting) held abstract in Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One; filtering content (BASCOM) found abstract under step 2A; considering historical usage while inputting data (BSG Tech. v. Buyseasons); mental processes a neurologist follows when testing a patient (In re Meyer); voting and vote verification/submission (Voter Verified v. Election Systems & Software) characterized as fundamental democratic activity; providing information without disrupting a person's primary activity (attention manager in Interval Licensing v. AOL) viewed as a basic nontechnical human activity; following rules/instructions such as game rules (In re Marco Guldenaar Holding B.V.) and hedging instructions (Bilski). Examiners should treat claims focused on organizing human activity and interpersonal behavior as potential abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes — general definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A mental process (thinking) that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using pen and paper, is considered an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative citations: CyberSource v. Retail Decisions; Gottschalk v. Benson; Mayo; Parker v. Flook. The grouping includes observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions and applies to product and process claims alike. Courts consider methods that are the equivalent of human mental work to be unpatentable abstract ideas (‘basic tools of scientific and technological work’). Examiners should use the subsequent points A–D to guide determination of whether a claim recites a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: A. Claim with limitation(s) that cannot practically be performed in the human mind does not recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim contains limitations that humans cannot practically perform mentally (the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not fall into the mental-process abstract-idea grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases/examples where claims were not mental processes because they could not practically be performed mentally: SRI Int’l v. Cisco (collection/analysis of network data using network monitors and packet analysis), SiRF Tech. (GPS pseudorange calculations to determine receiver position and time), Synopsys (specific multi-step data encryption manipulation), Research Corp. Techs. (pixel-by-pixel halftone rendering requiring manipulation of computer data structures). Examiners should identify limitations that a human cannot practically perform and treat those claims as not reciting a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: B. Claim that encompasses a human performing the step(s) mentally with or without a physical aid recites a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind — even if a physical aid (pen and paper, slide rule) may be used — the limitation falls within the mental-process grouping and is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts do not distinguish between purely mental acts and those aided by simple physical tools; the use of a physical aid does not negate the mental nature (Benson; Synopsys). Examples: CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card numbers could be done by writing transaction lists), Flook (computations performable by pencil and paper), University of Florida Research Foundation v. GE (analysis/manipulation described as performed mentally with pen and paper flowsheets and charts), Symantec (message screening steps performable mentally or with pen and paper). Examiners should consider whether claimed steps can be performed by a human mentally (possibly with simple aids) and, if so, treat them as mental processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: C. A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims implemented on a computer can nonetheless recite a mental process if the underlying claimed concept can be performed mentally (or with pen and paper); computer implementation alone does not avoid abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court/BCA cases: Benson (algorithm performable mentally but implemented in computers was an abstract idea); Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping could be performed by humans without a computer). Examiners should carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification to determine whether the applicant is simply claiming a concept performed 1) on a generic computer, 2) in a computer environment, or 3) using a computer as a tool — in those situations the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Example subpoint — Performing a mental process on a generic computer: Voter Verified (voting/verifying/submitting votes described as human cognitive actions despite computer implementation); Versata (determining a price using general purpose computer hardware). If the specification describes the claimed invention as a concept performed in the human mind and computer steps are generic, treat as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: D. ‘Mental processes’ is a type of abstract idea that can appear in product and process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The term ‘mental processes’ refers to a category of abstract ideas and is not limited to statutory claim types; product (systems, media) and process claims can both recite mental-process-type abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Versata (product claims to computer systems and computer-readable media were identified as reciting mental-process-type abstract ideas). Examiners should understand that the classification focuses on the nature of the idea, not whether the claim is a process or a product.
